## 15. Example lesson: what the learner actually does

### L0001 — Food and everyday meals: form and meaning

The first reference lesson begins with **bread, rice, water, milk, eat, drink**. The normalized module also provides the target chunks **have breakfast** and **drink water** for this lesson's eligible scope. Its initial grammar target is a simple subject–verb–object statement with `I/you/we/they`; later unit work extends the scope. The reference pack contains further language in context, but its mere presence is not an instruction to test an untaught grammatical rule.

The relevant material is embedded in §19 as **EX01** and available independently in `examples/EX01.md`.

| Step | Learner action | Concrete content / evidence |
|---|---|---|
| Intake | See the intended meaning, hear the word when audio exists, recognise a meaning | `bread`: a food made from flour and water and usually baked; `I eat bread.` |
| Dictation | Type from an aural cue, with the written answer absent | Expected forms include `bread`, `rice`, `water`, `milk`, `eat`, `drink`; recordings still need production |
| Context / relationship | Identify who performs the action and what they eat/drink | Do not confuse a food noun with the action verb |
| Grammar | Compare `I rice eat.` with `I eat rice.` | Explain the subject–verb–object relationship, then hide the model for repair |
| Chunk work | Retrieve the word partner in a meaningful situation | `drink water`; `have breakfast`; final cue/distractor authoring still required |
| Reading | Read the short account of Mina and Sam | “What does Mina eat in the morning? Write ONE WORD.” → `bread`, supported by the text |
| Listening | Hear the Ari/Jo exchange and follow the actual choice | The complete script and eight keyed teaching questions are supplied; natural audio is absent |
| Speaking | Produce a simple personal answer, not read the transcript | Record a relevant short response with intelligible familiar language |
| Writing | Write a small message about one meal | The reference task requests 20–40 words; this is not an IELTS Task 2 |
| Repair | Revisit only a diagnosed problem | Preserve the primary error; target spelling, meaning or the sentence relation as appropriate |
| Transfer | Use the capability on an unfamiliar small message | A new sealed task is required; the public example cannot serve as its own holdout |

This illustrates how topic, lexical targets, grammar, receptive text, productive response and correction fit together. It does **not** claim that one short lesson covers the complete food domain or establishes an IELTS band.

The other reference packs revisit food at increasing demands: quantities and orders; sequence; labels and comparisons; surplus systems; irrigation data; policy choices; resilience; uncertainty; innovation claims; competing criteria; and qualified synthesis. All example scenarios and numerical datasets are explicitly fictional teaching material, not facts about real programmes or research.

## 16. Implementation and content-production backlog

### 16.1 Priorities, with explicit acceptance conditions

| Priority | Work | Acceptance condition |
|---|---|---|
| P0 | Resolve authoring/runtime boundary | Verified final slide schemas, compiler mapping and focused contract tests; no guessed properties |
| P0 | Complete a pilot unit rather than publish the whole generated bank | Every target has reviewed content, complete tasks, working assets and valid evidence handling |
| P0 | Build trustworthy productive feedback | Qualitative evidence-based feedback first; numeric score estimates withheld until calibrated |
| P0 | Keep learning and assessment content separate | No answer keys or model responses leak into sealed attempts |
| P1 | Author the remaining lesson material packs | Original/licensed readings, scripts, recordings, visuals, keys and rationales meet the stage specifications |
| P1 | Validate the lexical and chunk inventories | Sense, grammatical behavior, register and useful partners verified; duplicates resolved by shared identity |
| P1 | Create the extensive input library | Meaning-focused graded reading/listening is genuinely available inside the app |
| P1 | Implement conditional repair recommendations | Error evidence selects the appropriate plan without changing scheduled Leitner semantics |
| P1 | Produce and calibrate full mock forms | Complete four-skill conditions and independent scoring evidence, not generic slide quizzes |
| P2 | Validate course-level placement and readiness routing | Decisions agree sufficiently with independent evidence and disclose uncertainty |
| P2 | Pilot and evaluate the complete course | Publish bounded outcome claims with transparent methods and limitations |

### 16.2 Instructions for a downstream content agent

Do not ingest `AUTHORING BRIEF` strings as if they were learner prompts. Take one lesson ID, inspect its source bank and prerequisite capabilities, author the missing material and attach evidence at the exercise level. Preserve the fixed opening and the original meaning of target relationships. Check the target coverage again after editing; a new passage can change the required lexical burden.

For a source-derived book lesson, inspect the actual authorized source rather than inventing its content from its title. For this original curriculum, construct new stimuli and label them original. Do not claim that a research paper supplied the words, facts or exact task order when it only supports a general learning principle.

Keep a lesson blocked until the required media and response evidence exist. Run the repository's authoritative validator in the checked-out repository when producing its final canonical authoring object; the independent checker in this package is not a replacement for that integration step. [V01, V06]

## 17. Files, reproducibility and validation

### 17.1 Package layout

```text
README.md                              Self-contained design, 960 lessons, examples, sources
data/
  modules.txt                          Original 120-unit lexical/chunk selections
  modules.normalized.json              Deduplicated normalized banks used by the build
  grammar.txt                          120 worked grammar/discourse diagnostics
  stages.json                          12 progressive demand profiles
  sources.json                         37-source evidence/provenance register
  lesson_index.jsonl                    960 lesson manifests and detailed asset briefs
  lesson_plans.jsonl                    960 canonical authoring objects, all production-blocked
  exercise_index.jsonl                  Expanded required/conditional exercise specifications
examples/
  EX01.md ... EX12.md                   Authored reference packs, one per stage
  reference_materials.json              Structured authored text, script, question and model data
stages/
  S01.md ... S12.md                     Smaller navigable copies of the lesson specifications
scripts/
  author_examples.py                    Rebuild the 12 authored packs
  build_course.py                      Expand the original curriculum design deterministically
  extract_lesson.py                     Extract one canonical object from the large JSONL bank
  validate_course.py                    Independent contract-oriented structural checks
  README-front.md                       Source of the narrative sections
  render_readme.py                      Optional HTML renderer (requires markdown-it-py)
  build_manifest.py                    Recompute hashes/counts and create the ZIP
audit/
  counts.json                          Actual computed counts, not promises
  validation.json                      Independent structural-check results and limitations
  manifest.json                        File hashes and sizes
```

`README.html` is a browser-readable copy with collapsible lesson sections. Only its optional renderer requires the third-party `markdown-it-py` package; the four core build/extraction/check commands below use the standard library. `audit/manifest.json` is authoritative about the files actually present. No audio asset or deployment binary should be inferred from an authoring reference string.

### 17.2 Rebuild and inspect

From the package directory, using Python 3.10 or later and the standard library:

```bash
python scripts/author_examples.py
python scripts/build_course.py
python scripts/validate_course.py
python scripts/extract_lesson.py L0001 --output lesson-L0001.json
```

`lesson_plans.jsonl` and `exercise_index.jsonl` are intentionally large. Stream them line by line instead of loading the entire exercise bank into a browser. The ZIP compresses repeated structural fields; it does not change the distinction between authored material and a design specification.

The build corrects a small set of duplicate strings within original unit rows and reorders the first food subset to match the authored reference pack. It writes those changes to the normalized bank rather than silently changing the source file. Repetition **across** units is intentional spiralling and is reported as occurrences versus distinct strings.

### 17.3 What the validation report establishes

The package checker verifies lesson/exercise/slide identity, allowed fields and slide types, exact opening scope, backward prerequisites, source/extension references, coverage unions, evidence IDs, declared material blockers and reproducible counts. It also checks the authored reference-pack structure and relevant writing-model minimums.

It is an **independent checker implemented for this deliverable against the inspected contract**. It is not represented as a successful execution of the repository's own validator or a full application integration test. It does not prove pedagogical correctness, validate all distractors, create missing media, calibrate scores or demonstrate learning outcomes.

The final `audit/validation.json` records exactly which checks passed and which limitations remain. A positive structural result must always be read alongside `runtime_ready_lessons: 0` and the explicit `blocked` status of each lesson object.

## 18. All 960 lesson specifications

Each lesson below has a matching canonical authoring object in `data/lesson_plans.jsonl` and a complete exercise manifest in `data/lesson_index.jsonl`. These are target-specific specifications, not claims that all their stimuli and answer banks already exist. Core development and optional repair are counted separately.

### Stage 01 — Build usable sentences

**Scaffolding:** Brief optional first-language explanation, illustrated meaning, model sentence and replay in learning mode; remove them for the final retrieval.

**Reading envelope:** 60–120 words. **Listening envelope:** 25–60 seconds. These are authoring policies for integrated tasks, not validated band boundaries; a focused extract may be shorter.

**Progression evidence:** Demonstrate short-text comprehension and independent simple production; early band labels are curriculum orientation, not a scored IELTS conversion.

#### L0001 · Food and everyday meals — Form and meaning
**Purpose:** Establish a usable lexical representation and use it in a simple communicative exchange. **Prerequisite:** entry diagnostic / foundation bridge. Introduce this subset; reuse shared vocabulary identities.
**Vocabulary:** bread, rice, water, milk, eat, drink.
**Collocations:** have breakfast; drink water.
**Grammar / discourse:** Subject + present-tense verb + object with I/you/we/they; Object nouns; receptive recognition of eats/drinks with named subjects; capital I and final full stop.
**Worked diagnostic:** `I rice eat.` → `I eat rice.` Place the finite verb after the subject in this simple statement. Rice is the object.
**Reading:** Find explicitly stated people, actions, objects and locations in short texts. Family: `short-answer`.
**Listening:** Recognise familiar words and retrieve a stated item, number or place without relying on the transcript. Family: `form-completion`. **Sound focus:** Word boundaries, stressed syllables, clear final consonants and meaningful pauses.
**Speaking:** Say what you eat and drink in the morning. Use two or three complete statements. You may invent a meal. Do not read the model.
**Writing:** Write 20–40 words about one meal. Say who eats, what they eat and what they drink. Use the six target words where relevant; do not force all of them.

### Stage 02 — Manage everyday exchanges

**Scaffolding:** One worked example per new operation; optional replay before a fresh no-transcript attempt.

**Reading envelope:** 100–180 words. **Listening envelope:** 40–90 seconds. These are authoring policies for integrated tasks, not validated band boundaries; a focused extract may be shorter.

**Progression evidence:** Complete unseen everyday tasks without copying a model; retain earlier sentence patterns across changed topics.

#### L0081 · Shopping for ingredients — Form and meaning
**Purpose:** Establish a usable lexical representation and use it in a simple communicative exchange. **Prerequisite:** L0080. Introduce this subset; reuse shared vocabulary identities.
**Vocabulary:** ingredient, vegetable, carrot, onion, pepper, cheese.
**Collocations:** a kilo of rice; a bottle of oil.
**Grammar / discourse:** Count and mass nouns with some/any; How much/how many; containers and quantities.
**Worked diagnostic:** `How many rice do we need?` → `How much rice do we need?` Rice is a mass noun in this context; ask how much, or count bags or bowls.
**Reading:** Follow instructions, locate quantities and distinguish routines from current actions. Family: `short-answer`.
**Listening:** Complete a simple form from a two-speaker exchange and track a correction. Family: `form-completion`. **Sound focus:** Plural endings, contracted forms, weak function words and question intonation.
**Speaking:** Role-play a shop order. Ask for two ingredients, specify a quantity, then politely correct one part of your order. Answer a follow-up about payment.
**Writing:** Write 40–65 words explaining what you need for a simple meal and what you already have. Use some/any and one countable quantity.

### Stage 03 — Narrate, compare and explain

**Scaffolding:** Keyword notes rather than full scripts; gradually remove sentence starters.

**Reading envelope:** 160–260 words. **Listening envelope:** 60–120 seconds. These are authoring policies for integrated tasks, not validated band boundaries; a focused extract may be shorter.

**Progression evidence:** Control past/present reference and give relevant reasons in unfamiliar everyday contexts.

#### L0161 · Cooking and eating together — Form and meaning
**Purpose:** Establish a usable lexical representation and use it in a simple communicative exchange. **Prerequisite:** L0160. Introduce this subset; reuse shared vocabulary identities.
**Vocabulary:** recipe, portion, slice, piece, bowl, plate.
**Collocations:** follow a recipe; chop vegetables.
**Grammar / discourse:** Past simple regular verbs; Past time reference; -ed pronunciation as a separate aural target.
**Worked diagnostic:** `We cook dinner yesterday.` → `We cooked dinner yesterday.` Use the past form cooked for the completed event yesterday.
**Reading:** Identify chronology, compare options and support a literal answer with a precise text span. Family: `short-answer`.
**Listening:** Follow a sequence and distinguish an initial suggestion from the final decision. Family: `form-completion`. **Sound focus:** Regular past endings, irregular verb recognition and phrase-level stress.
**Speaking:** Describe a meal you made or an imaginary meal. Explain the sequence and one problem. Speak for 45–70 seconds. Answer: What would you do differently next time?
**Writing:** Write 70–100 words about a cooking activity. Use past simple for the main events and one while-clause for a simultaneous action.

### Stage 04 — Connect ideas and follow arguments

**Scaffolding:** Teach the question mechanics on a different text; progressively delay feedback until task submission.

**Reading envelope:** 230–360 words. **Listening envelope:** 90–180 seconds. These are authoring policies for integrated tasks, not validated band boundaries; a focused extract may be shorter.

**Progression evidence:** Preserve the source meaning, complete coherent tasks and distinguish knowledge gaps from careless answer-format errors.

#### L0241 · Food choices and simple nutrition — Form and meaning
**Purpose:** Establish a usable lexical representation and use it in a simple communicative exchange. **Prerequisite:** L0240. Introduce this subset; reuse shared vocabulary identities.
**Vocabulary:** nutrition, nutrient, protein, carbohydrate, fat, fibre.
**Collocations:** food label; portion size.
**Grammar / discourse:** Countability in food and abstract nouns; Few/a few; little/a little without equating their meanings.
**Worked diagnostic:** `There are little informations on the label.` → `There is little information on the label.` Information is normally uncountable; use is and do not add plural -s.
**Reading:** Track reference and cause; distinguish explicit contradiction from missing information. Family: `sentence-completion`.
**Listening:** Identify key details, speaker intentions and changes of plan in short sustained audio. Family: `note-completion`. **Sound focus:** Linking, contrastive stress, prominent content words and self-monitoring of intelligibility.
**Speaking:** Explain why two labels or prices can be difficult to compare. Give an example and identify one thing that the information does not establish. Speak for 60–90 seconds.
**Writing:** Write 100–150 words explaining the label-comparison activity. Include the initial error, the correction and one limitation. Do not give medical advice or invent nutrient figures.
**Ordered required exercises** (numbers in parentheses are authoring slides): L0241-E01: Vocabulary intake (16) → L0241-E02: Spelling and dictation (8) → L0241-E03: Sense, context and word relationships (2) → L0241-E04: Notice the sentence relationship (2) → L0241-E05: Use the relationship in a different message (1) → L0241-E06: Retrieve natural word partners (2) → L0241-E07: Recognise the prepared language in speech (2) → L0241-E08: Read an intact text and justify meaning (9) → L0241-E09: Listen to a coherent message (9) → L0241-E10: Contrast two plausible senses (2) → L0241-E11: Retrieve without recognition options (2) → L0241-E12: Plan briefly and communicate independently (2) → L0241-E13: Plan, draft and preserve the first response (2) → L0241-E14: Notice, revise and explain one change (2) → L0241-E23: Independent cumulative check (6).
**Conditional repair bank:** 8 target-specific two-slide repairs, one for each eligible word/chunk; see IDs L0241-E15–L0241-E22. These are not compulsory repetitions. Routing is a proposed extension.
**Gate and error rule:** G1 for this lesson; G2 also at role 8. Preserve first attempt; diagnose; repair only the failed dimension; use a different cue at recheck; use existing Leitner scheduling. No feedback inside the final coherent scored task.

#### L0249 · Living arrangements and responsibilities — Form and meaning

**Vocabulary:** disagreement, misunderstanding, personality, behaviour, attitude, mood, support, apologise, forgive, persuade, refuse, accept.
**Collocations:** build trust; keep in touch; have an argument; resolve a disagreement; make an apology; offer support.
**Grammar / discourse:** Present perfect versus past simple; Since/for; finished versus unfinished reference periods.
**Worked diagnostic:** `I know her since five years.` → `I have known her for five years.` Use present perfect for the continuing state, and for with a duration.
**Reading:** Track reference and cause; distinguish explicit contradiction from missing information. Family: `matching-headings`.
**Listening:** Identify key details, speaker intentions and changes of plan in short sustained audio. Family: `multiple-choice-single`. **Sound focus:** Linking, contrastive stress, prominent content words and self-monitoring of intelligibility.
**Speaking:** Speak about Relationships and communication for 60–90 seconds in this focused drill. State a relevant answer, develop it at stage 4, and use suitable prepared language naturally. Do not force all chunks: build trust; keep in touch; have an argument; resolve a disagreement; make an apology; offer support.
**Writing:** Write 90–150 words about Relationships and communication. Communicative aim: Organise two connected paragraphs; begin describing data and reporting a process. Use prepared language naturally; this is a scaffolded training task, not a complete IELTS Writing task.

### Stage 05 — Enter sustained IELTS-style tasks

**Scaffolding:** Planning frames optional during learning only; guided tasks and fresh timed tasks use different facts.

**Reading envelope:** 320–470 words. **Listening envelope:** 120–240 seconds. These are authoring policies for integrated tasks, not validated band boundaries; a focused extract may be shorter.

**Progression evidence:** Attempt complete IELTS-style task shapes with explicit gap diagnosis rather than inflated projected bands.

#### L0321 · Food waste and responsible consumption — Form and meaning
**Purpose:** Establish a usable lexical representation and use it in a simple communicative exchange. **Prerequisite:** L0320. Introduce this subset; reuse shared vocabulary identities.
**Vocabulary:** surplus, shortage, expiry, storage, preservation, distribution.
**Collocations:** food waste; expiry date.
**Grammar / discourse:** Second conditional; Would + base form; hypothetical versus realistic conditions.
**Worked diagnostic:** `If shops would donate more food, less would be wasted.` → `If shops donated more food, less would be wasted.` In the standard hypothetical pattern, the if-clause uses past simple rather than would.
**Reading:** Identify paragraph purpose, paraphrase and supporting detail without searching for exact word repetition. Family: `sentence-completion`.
**Listening:** Follow everyday and study-related exchanges across a complete question block. Family: `note-completion`. **Sound focus:** Multiword chunks, reduced forms, emphasis and intelligible multi-clause delivery.
**Speaking:** Describe a local scheme that tries to solve a practical problem. Explain its goal, one difficulty and a better way to measure success. Speak for up to two minutes.
**Writing:** Write 150–200 words answering: Is collecting surplus food enough to solve food waste? Use the fictional trial as an example, distinguish prevention from redistribution and acknowledge a limitation.

### Stage 06 — Build independent four-skill performance

**Scaffolding:** Task plan rather than language template; gradual transition to 20/40-minute writing budgets.

**Reading envelope:** 420–650 words. **Listening envelope:** 180–300 seconds. These are authoring policies for integrated tasks, not validated band boundaries; a focused extract may be shorter.

**Progression evidence:** Produce sustained independent work in all four skills; keep skill scores separate.

#### L0401 · Agriculture and food supply — Form and meaning
**Purpose:** Establish a usable lexical representation and use it in a simple communicative exchange. **Prerequisite:** L0400. Introduce this subset; reuse shared vocabulary identities.
**Vocabulary:** agriculture, cultivation, harvest, crop, yield, irrigation.
**Collocations:** crop yield; food supply.
**Grammar / discourse:** Third conditional; Past counterfactuals; had + participle and would have + participle.
**Worked diagnostic:** `If storage would have improved, less food would have spoiled.` → `If storage had improved, less food would have spoiled.` The standard counterfactual if-clause uses had improved.
**Reading:** Summarise relationships between claims, evidence and examples in extended prose. Family: `sentence-completion`.
**Listening:** Follow educational discussion and a short lecture with reduced replay support. Family: `note-completion`. **Sound focus:** Natural pacing, clause boundaries, correction without repeated restarting and accent variation.
**Speaking:** Explain why two systems can each be better on different measures. Use the irrigation comparison, then give another example. Respond to the follow-up: How should a decision-maker choose between the measures?
**Writing:** Academic Task 1-style practice: summarise the fictional data in at least 150 words. A: water 1,000, yield 200; B: water 800, yield 190. Include an overview and accurate comparisons. Do not infer costs, profitability or causation.

**Progression evidence:** Show repeatable transfer beyond rehearsed topics and reduce persistent error families.

#### L0481 · Food policy and competing priorities — Form and meaning
**Purpose:** Establish a usable lexical representation and use it in a simple communicative exchange. **Prerequisite:** L0480. Introduce this subset; reuse shared vocabulary identities.
**Vocabulary:** subsidy, regulation, taxation, incentive, affordability, availability.
**Collocations:** food policy; economic incentive.
**Grammar / discourse:** Modals and counterarguments in policy; Should/ought to; proportionate obligation and exceptions.
**Worked diagnostic:** `Labels should must be clear.` → `Labels should be clear, although the policy may need exceptions.` Do not stack these modal verbs; select one appropriate expression of obligation.
**Reading:** Track scope, qualification, author stance and similarities across paraphrases. Family: `true-false-not-given`.
**Listening:** Track agreement, disagreement and attributed opinions in educational discussions. Family: `table-completion`. **Sound focus:** Prosodic grouping, contrast, unobtrusive self-repair and intelligibility during extended explanations.
**Speaking:** Discuss whether lower prices are enough to make a service accessible. Explain two other barriers and respond to a follow-up that challenges your proposed solution.
**Writing:** Task 2-style practice: Some people believe governments should reduce the price of healthier food. Others think consumers should make food choices without government intervention. Discuss both views and give your own opinion. Write at least 250 words. Do not invent research or statistics.

#### L0561 · Global food systems — Form and meaning
**Purpose:** Establish a usable lexical representation and use it in a simple communicative exchange. **Prerequisite:** L0560. Introduce this subset; reuse shared vocabulary identities.
**Vocabulary:** interdependence, resilience, volatility, distribution, scarcity, surplus.
**Collocations:** food security; supply-chain resilience.
**Grammar / discourse:** Precision in complex noun phrases; Resolve stacked modifiers before writing; use of-phrases where clearer.
**Worked diagnostic:** `The regional food supply resilience improvement improved.` → `The resilience of the regional food supply improved.` Reduce nominal piling and make the central claim explicit.
**Reading:** Distinguish claims from evidence and interpret implication without importing outside knowledge. Family: `true-false-not-given`.
**Listening:** Follow extended argument and retain the final position after concessions and corrections. Family: `table-completion`. **Sound focus:** Flexible emphasis and phrasing; recognise unfamiliar voices without assuming a single preferred accent.
**Speaking:** Is an efficient system necessarily a reliable one? Develop a position, acknowledge a counterexample and explain what information would change your view.
**Writing:** Task 2-style practice: Some organisations aim to minimise costs, while others keep spare capacity to deal with unexpected problems. Discuss both approaches and give your opinion. Write at least 250 words.
**Ordered required exercises** (numbers in parentheses are authoring slides): L0561-E01: Vocabulary intake (16) → L0561-E02: Spelling and dictation (8) → L0561-E03: Sense, context and word relationships (2) → L0561-E04: Notice the sentence relationship (2) → L0561-E05: Use the relationship in a different message (1) → L0561-E06: Retrieve natural word partners (2) → L0561-E07: Recognise the prepared language in speech (2) → L0561-E08: Read an intact text and justify meaning (9) → L0561-E09: Listen to a coherent message (9) → L0561-E10: Contrast two plausible senses (2) → L0561-E11: Retrieve without recognition options (2) → L0561-E12: Plan briefly and communicate independently (2) → L0561-E13: Plan, draft and preserve the first response (2) → L0561-E14: Notice, revise and explain one change (2) → L0561-E23: Independent cumulative check (6).
**Conditional repair bank:** 8 target-specific two-slide repairs, one for each eligible word/chunk; see IDs L0561-E15–L0561-E22. These are not compulsory repetitions. Routing is a proposed extension.

### Stage 09 — Handle nuance and unfamiliarity

**Scaffolding:** Targeted micro-repair between complete performances, not hints inside an assessment.

**Reading envelope:** 650–950 words. **Listening envelope:** 240–420 seconds. These are authoring policies for integrated tasks, not validated band boundaries; a focused extract may be shorter.

#### L0641 · Food systems under uncertainty — Form and meaning
**Purpose:** Establish a usable lexical representation and use it in a simple communicative exchange. **Prerequisite:** L0640. Introduce this subset; reuse shared vocabulary identities.
**Vocabulary:** resilience, vulnerability, diversification, contingency, buffer, volatility.
**Collocations:** supply disruption; contingency planning.
**Grammar / discourse:** Counterfactual reasoning and conditional limits; Were it not for; equivalent plain alternatives remain acceptable.
**Worked diagnostic:** `Without the reserve, the shortage will have been worse yesterday.` → `Without the reserve, the shortage would have been worse.` Use a coherent past hypothetical consequence rather than a future-perfect form.
**Reading:** Resolve ambiguity, trace alternative explanations and avoid overgeneralising a qualified statement. Family: `true-false-not-given`.
**Listening:** Infer attitude from wording and prosody while preserving what is explicitly versus implicitly supported. Family: `table-completion`. **Sound focus:** Meaningful intonation, listener-friendly pace and adaptation to unfamiliar speakers.
**Speaking:** Should decision-makers wait for certainty before acting? Give a balanced answer, distinguish useful estimates from guarantees and explain how a provisional decision can be reviewed.
**Writing:** Task 2-style practice: Some people think decisions should only be made when enough information is available. Others believe waiting for more information often causes greater problems. Discuss both views and give your own opinion. Write at least 250 words.

### Stage 10 — Prioritise precision and control

**Scaffolding:** Models shown only after the independent attempt; blind compare and justify revisions.

**Reading envelope:** 700–1000 words. **Listening envelope:** 240–420 seconds. These are authoring policies for integrated tasks, not validated band boundaries; a focused extract may be shorter.

**Progression evidence:** High performance must persist on unseen tasks; a model answer imitation is not evidence of independent ability.

#### L0721 · Agricultural innovation and evidence — Form and meaning
**Purpose:** Establish a usable lexical representation and use it in a simple communicative exchange. **Prerequisite:** L0720. Introduce this subset; reuse shared vocabulary identities.
**Vocabulary:** innovation, diffusion, adoption, productivity, resilience, externality.
**Collocations:** sustainable intensification; adoption barrier.
**Grammar / discourse:** Dense but controlled technical explanation; Define specialist nouns through accessible paraphrase.
**Worked diagnostic:** `The method increased yield, meaning farmers became richer in every case.` → `The method increased yield, meaning the amount harvested per area.` A definition of yield is not a claim about universal income effects.
**Reading:** Interpret dense prose, distinguish methodological limits and verify each inference against evidence. Family: `matching-headings`.
**Listening:** Track layered positions, implicit qualification and lecture organisation with one examination playback. Family: `multiple-choice-single`. **Sound focus:** Consistent intelligibility, flexible stress and smooth spontaneous reformulation.
**Speaking:** A pilot programme has promising results but several limitations. Should it be expanded? Develop a conditional recommendation and respond to the challenge: Are you being too cautious?
**Writing:** Task 2-style practice: New technologies are often introduced widely after small trials. Some people think this encourages progress, while others believe stronger evidence should be required first. Discuss both views and give your opinion. Write at least 250 words.

#### L0761 · Transport appraisal and uncertainty — Form and meaning
**Purpose:** Establish a usable lexical representation and use it in a simple communicative exchange. **Prerequisite:** L0760. Introduce this subset; reuse shared vocabulary identities.
**Vocabulary:** appraisal, forecast, sensitivity, scenario, uncertainty, discount rate.
**Collocations:** sensitivity analysis; demand uncertainty.
**Grammar / discourse:** Conditional clauses with probabilistic forecasts; Distinguish expected values from guaranteed outcomes.

#### L0801 · Resilience versus efficiency in food systems — Form and meaning
**Purpose:** Establish a usable lexical representation and use it in a simple communicative exchange. **Prerequisite:** L0800. Introduce this subset; reuse shared vocabulary identities.
**Vocabulary:** resilience, efficiency, redundancy, optimisation, vulnerability, robustness.
**Collocations:** system resilience; productive efficiency.
**Grammar / discourse:** Synthesis across evidence and constraints; Concession integrated into a single coherent position.
**Worked diagnostic:** `Greater redundancy reduces efficiency, so resilience cannot improve.` → `Greater redundancy may reduce efficiency while improving resilience.` The two outcomes can move in different directions; retain the trade-off.
**Reading:** Resolve fine distinctions, evaluate competing interpretations and retain exact scope under time pressure. Family: `matching-headings`.
**Listening:** Recognise shifts in stance and rapidly recover after a missed detail without losing the next answer. Family: `multiple-choice-single`. **Sound focus:** Stable connected speech, unobtrusive repair, precise focus and effortless listener comprehension.
**Speaking:** Explain a situation in which two reasonable objectives conflict. Propose a compromise, state its conditions and respond to a challenge that your proposal is neither ambitious enough nor cheap enough.
**Writing:** Task 2-style practice: Organisations should always choose the most efficient way of operating, even if this leaves little spare capacity. To what extent do you agree or disagree? Write at least 250 words.

**Reading envelope:** 700–1000 words. **Listening envelope:** 240–420 seconds. These are authoring policies for integrated tasks, not validated band boundaries; a focused extract may be shorter.

**Progression evidence:** A conditional readiness decision requires multiple independent fresh performances and valid scoring. An actual IELTS result remains the examination outcome.

#### L0881 · Food-system decisions: expert transfer — Form and meaning
**Purpose:** Establish a usable lexical representation and use it in a simple communicative exchange. **Prerequisite:** L0880. Introduce this subset; reuse shared vocabulary identities.
**Vocabulary:** contingency, resilience, distribution, legitimacy, uncertainty, externality.
**Collocations:** defensible judgement; proportionate intervention.
**Grammar / discourse:** Flexible grammatical choice under time pressure; Choose the simplest precise form; no mandatory complexity quota.
**Worked diagnostic:** `The policy is promising, provided that its effects is monitored.` → `The policy is promising, provided that its effects are monitored.` Agreement must remain accurate even inside a subordinate clause.
**Reading:** Achieve near-complete supported comprehension on varied unseen passages and all question families. Family: `matching-headings`.
**Listening:** Achieve near-complete comprehension on varied unseen natural recordings and all question families. Family: `multiple-choice-single`. **Sound focus:** Natural, flexible, intelligible speech whose accent does not obstruct understanding.
**Speaking:** Complete a simulated Part 3 exchange. Main question: How should institutions make decisions when the evidence is incomplete? Follow-ups: Can too much caution be harmful? Who should decide acceptable trade-offs? What would make you change your recommendation? Answer spontaneously; do not deliver a prepared essay.
**Writing:** Task 2-style practice: Institutions should prioritise lower costs when choosing services, even when this reduces flexibility or affects other organisations. To what extent do you agree or disagree? Write at least 250 words. Address the extent of agreement explicitly and avoid invented evidence.

## 19. Twelve authored reference packs

These complete **reference packs** contain original texts, scripts and keyed questions. They illustrate a spiral in one domain; they do not replace the missing 948 lesson material packs, natural recordings, full mock forms or productive scoring calibration. Their questions are public teaching material and may never be reused as sealed readiness evidence.

<details>
<summary>EX01: Food: who eats what?</summary>

### EX01 — Food: who eats what?

Original Vocora-commissioned fictional teaching material; not an IELTS test or a certified band exemplar.

Associated design lesson: **L0001**. Status: **authored reference pack, not a complete runtime lesson**.

#### Target lexicon

| Target | Role | Meaning | Original example |

|---|---|---|---|

| bread | noun, normally uncountable in this meaning | a food made from flour and water and usually baked | I eat bread. |

| rice | uncountable noun | small grains cooked and eaten as food | We eat rice. |

| water | uncountable noun | the clear liquid people drink | I drink water. |

| milk | uncountable noun | a white liquid used as a drink or food | We drink milk. |

| eat | verb | to put food in your mouth and swallow it | I eat rice. |

| drink | verb | to take liquid into your mouth and swallow it | You drink water. |



**Word partners:** eat bread; eat rice; drink water


#### Reading stimulus

My name is Mina. I eat bread in the morning. I drink milk. My brother, Sam, eats rice at lunch. He drinks water. We eat at home. Our table is small. In the evening, I eat rice and Sam eats bread. We both drink water. We like our meals. On Sunday, our friend Jo eats with us at home.


#### Listening script — audio not yet recorded

Ari: Hello, Jo. What do you eat in the morning?
Jo: I eat rice.
Ari: Do you drink milk?
Jo: No. I drink water.
Ari: I eat bread and drink milk.
Jo: Do you eat at home?
Ari: Yes. My sister eats with me.
Jo: I eat with my brother. We sit at a small table.


#### Reading questions and answer rationales

##### EX01-R01 · `short-answer`

What does Mina eat in the morning? Write ONE WORD.

**Answer:** bread

**Why:** The second sentence states Mina eats bread in the morning.

##### EX01-R02 · `short-answer`

What does Sam drink at lunch? Write ONE WORD.

**Answer:** water

**Why:** He in the sentence after Sam refers to Sam.

##### EX01-R03 · `truth`

Mina and Sam eat at home. TRUE, FALSE or NOT GIVEN?

**Answer:** TRUE

**Why:** We eat at home explicitly states this.

##### EX01-R04 · `truth`

Their table is large. TRUE, FALSE or NOT GIVEN?

**Answer:** FALSE

**Why:** The text says the table is small.

##### EX01-R05 · `truth`

Jo is twenty years old. TRUE, FALSE or NOT GIVEN?

**Answer:** NOT GIVEN

**Why:** The text gives no age for Jo.

##### EX01-R06 · `classification`

In I eat bread, identify the subject, verb and object.

**Answer:** I = subject; eat = verb; bread = object

**Why:** The subject does the action, and bread names what is eaten.

##### EX01-R07 · `short-answer`

Who eats with the family on Sunday? Write ONE WORD.

**Answer:** Jo

**Why:** The last sentence identifies the visitor.

##### EX01-R08 · `short-answer`

What do both Mina and Sam drink in the evening? Write ONE WORD.

**Answer:** water

**Why:** We both drink water follows the evening meal description.


#### Listening questions and answer rationales

##### EX01-A01 · `short-answer`

What does Jo eat in the morning? ONE WORD.

**Answer:** rice

**Why:** Jo says I eat rice.

##### EX01-A02 · `short-answer`

What does Jo drink? ONE WORD.

**Answer:** water

**Why:** Jo rejects milk and states water.

##### EX01-A03 · `short-answer`

What does Ari eat? ONE WORD.

**Answer:** bread

**Why:** Ari explicitly says I eat bread.

##### EX01-A04 · `short-answer`

What does Ari drink? ONE WORD.

**Answer:** milk

**Why:** Ari says drink milk.

##### EX01-A05 · `choice`

Who eats with Ari: his sister, his brother, or Jo?

**Answer:** his sister

**Why:** Ari says My sister eats with me.

##### EX01-A06 · `choice`

Who eats with Jo: her teacher, her brother, or Mina?

**Answer:** her brother

**Why:** Jo names her brother.

##### EX01-A07 · `truth`

Jo says she drinks milk. TRUE or FALSE?

**Answer:** FALSE

**Why:** No rejects the suggested milk; water is the final answer.

##### EX01-A08 · `dictation`

Listen to the isolated phrase from a separate word-audio cue and type it: drink water.

**Answer:** drink water

**Why:** Exact word form and boundary, not a comprehension inference.


#### Speaking

Say what you eat and drink in the morning. Use two or three complete statements. You may invent a meal. Do not read the model.


#### Writing

Write 20–40 words about one meal. Say who eats, what they eat and what they drink. Use the six target words where relevant; do not force all of them.


##### Original model — show after submission

I eat bread in the morning. I drink water. My sister eats rice. She drinks milk. We eat at home, and we like our food.


#### Design and assessment note

Teach I/you/we, the core SVO frame, and eat versus drink before the reading. Names, home, morning and table must be known from onboarding or glossed. Third-person forms in the passage are supported exposure, not an untaught compulsory production target. TRUE/FALSE/NOT GIVEN here is guided logic practice, not a timed IELTS test.


**Evidence for the operations, not certification of this pack:** I02, I03, I04, I05, I06, I07, R01, R03, R04, R06, R07. See the source ledger in README.md.

<summary>EX02: Shopping: quantities and the final order</summary>

### EX02 — Shopping: quantities and the final order

Original Vocora-commissioned fictional teaching material; not an IELTS test or a certified band exemplar.

Associated design lesson: **L0081**. Status: **authored reference pack, not a complete runtime lesson**.

#### Target lexicon

| Target | Role | Meaning | Original example |

|---|---|---|---|

| ingredient | count noun | one of the foods used to make a dish | Rice is one ingredient in this meal. |

| vegetable | count noun | a plant or part of a plant eaten as food | We buy fresh vegetables. |

| carrot | count noun | a long orange vegetable | We need two carrots. |

| onion | count noun | a vegetable with layers and a strong taste | Chop one onion. |

| pepper | count noun in this context | a red, green or yellow vegetable | Add a red pepper. |

| cheese | normally uncountable noun | a food made from milk | We need some cheese. |



**Word partners:** a kilo of rice; a bottle of oil; pay in cash


#### Reading stimulus

The neighbourhood cooking club meets on Saturday. This week, six people are making a vegetable meal. Leila has a shopping list. She needs one kilo of rice, four carrots, two onions and one red pepper. There is already some oil in the club kitchen, so she does not need to buy a bottle. The club also has salt. Leila wants some cheese for a small salad, but the shop does not have any today. She decides to make the salad without it. The vegetables cost eight pounds, and the rice costs three pounds. Leila pays eleven pounds in cash. She keeps the receipt. The club starts cooking at ten, but Leila arrives at half past nine to wash the vegetables. The club is next to the library. The notice does not give the library's opening time.


#### Listening script — audio not yet recorded

Shopkeeper: Good morning. What would you like?
Customer: Two kilos of rice, please. Sorry, just one kilo. There are only three of us today.
Shopkeeper: One kilo. Anything else?
Customer: Three onions and a bottle of oil.
Shopkeeper: The small bottle or the large one?
Customer: The small one, please. Do you have any carrots?
Shopkeeper: Yes. They are two pounds a kilo.
Customer: I'll take one kilo of carrots as well.
Shopkeeper: That is nine pounds in total.
Customer: Can I pay by card?
Shopkeeper: I'm sorry, the machine is not working.
Customer: That's all right. I'll pay in cash. Could I have a receipt?
Shopkeeper: Of course. Here you are.


#### Reading questions and answer rationales

##### EX02-R01 · `short-answer`

How many people are cooking on Saturday? ONE WORD OR A NUMBER.

**Answer:** six / 6

**Why:** The second sentence gives six.

##### EX02-R02 · `short-answer`

How many onions are on Leila's list? ONE WORD OR A NUMBER.

**Answer:** two / 2

**Why:** The list says two onions.

##### EX02-R03 · `truth`

Leila buys some oil. TRUE, FALSE or NOT GIVEN?

**Answer:** FALSE

**Why:** Oil is already available, so she does not buy it.

##### EX02-R04 · `truth`

The shop has cheese today. TRUE, FALSE or NOT GIVEN?

**Answer:** FALSE

**Why:** It does not have any today.

##### EX02-R05 · `short-answer`

What is the total cost in pounds? ONE WORD OR A NUMBER.

**Answer:** eleven / 11

**Why:** Eight for vegetables plus three for rice equals eleven.

##### EX02-R06 · `short-answer`

At what time does Leila arrive? Write a time.

**Answer:** 9:30 / half past nine

**Why:** Arrival is earlier than the ten o'clock cooking start.

##### EX02-R07 · `truth`

The library opens at nine. TRUE, FALSE or NOT GIVEN?

**Answer:** NOT GIVEN

**Why:** The text explicitly says the opening time is not given.

##### EX02-R08 · `error-correction`

Correct only the quantity question: How many rice does Leila buy?

**Answer:** How much rice does Leila buy?

**Why:** Rice is uncountable here; kilos would be countable.


#### Listening questions and answer rationales

##### EX02-A01 · `short-answer`

Final rice order, in kilos: ONE WORD OR A NUMBER.

**Answer:** one / 1

**Why:** Two is explicitly corrected to one.

##### EX02-A02 · `short-answer`

Number of onions: ONE WORD OR A NUMBER.

**Answer:** three / 3

**Why:** The customer orders three onions.

##### EX02-A03 · `short-answer`

Oil bottle size: ONE WORD.

**Answer:** small

**Why:** The customer chooses the small bottle.

##### EX02-A04 · `short-answer`

Carrots cost ___ pounds a kilo. ONE WORD OR A NUMBER.

**Answer:** two / 2

**Why:** This is the unit price, not the total purchase price.

##### EX02-A05 · `short-answer`

Total cost: ___ pounds. ONE WORD OR A NUMBER.

**Answer:** nine / 9

**Why:** The shopkeeper states the total.

##### EX02-A06 · `choice`

How does the customer finally pay: card, cash, or online transfer?

**Answer:** cash

**Why:** Card is requested but unavailable; cash is the final method.

##### EX02-A07 · `short-answer`

What document does the customer request? ONE WORD.

**Answer:** receipt

**Why:** Could I have a receipt? provides the exact word.

##### EX02-A08 · `choice`

Why is the rice order reduced: fewer people, a higher price, or no rice in stock?

**Answer:** fewer people

**Why:** The customer says there are only three people today.


#### Speaking

Role-play a shop order. Ask for two ingredients, specify a quantity, then politely correct one part of your order. Answer a follow-up about payment.


#### Writing

Write 40–65 words explaining what you need for a simple meal and what you already have. Use some/any and one countable quantity.


##### Original model — show after submission

We are making a vegetable meal for three people. We need one kilo of rice, two onions and some carrots. We already have some oil, so we do not need another bottle. There is not any cheese in the kitchen, but we can make the meal without it.


#### Design and assessment note

The teaching passage and listening order use different people, quantities and final decisions. For a test, hide the script and do not reveal the corrected order beforehand. A synthetic dialogue is acceptable for formative rehearsal only; a readiness task needs natural, quality-controlled audio.

### EX03 — Cooking: reconstructing a sequence

Original Vocora-commissioned fictional teaching material; not an IELTS test or a certified band exemplar.

Associated design lesson: **L0161**. Status: **authored reference pack, not a complete runtime lesson**.

#### Target lexicon

| Target | Role | Meaning | Original example |

|---|---|---|---|

| recipe | count noun | instructions for making a particular dish | We followed a simple recipe. |

| portion | count noun | an amount of food for one person | The recipe makes four portions. |

| slice | count noun | a thin flat piece cut from something | She cut a slice of bread. |

| piece | count noun | a part separated from a whole | Add a small piece of cheese. |

| bowl | count noun | a round container for food | Put the salad in a bowl. |

| plate | count noun | a flat dish for serving food | The bread is on a plate. |



**Word partners:** follow a recipe; chop vegetables; a bowl of soup


#### Reading stimulus

Last month, Dan joined a cooking class because he wanted to prepare meals without buying expensive ready-made food. In the first lesson, the class made vegetable soup. The teacher gave everyone the same recipe, but asked each pair to choose one extra vegetable. Dan and his partner chose carrots.

First, they washed the vegetables and chopped them into small pieces. They then heated a little oil in a pan and cooked the onions for five minutes. After that, they added the other vegetables and some water. The soup cooked for twenty minutes. While they were waiting, Dan cut some bread and his partner set the table.

The recipe made four portions. There were only two people in each pair, so they put the remaining soup in labelled containers to take home. Dan thought his soup needed more salt, but the teacher suggested tasting it again before adding anything. He followed her advice and decided not to add more.

At the end of the class, each pair described one problem and one useful skill. Dan said that cutting the vegetables into similar-sized pieces was difficult at first. However, he was pleased that he could now explain the cooking process to someone else. The class was not a competition, and nobody received a prize.


#### Listening script — audio not yet recorded

Tutor: Tell me about the meal your pair made yesterday.
Nora: We made a salad and baked some bread. We started with the bread because it needed more time.
Tutor: What did you do first?
Nora: We mixed the flour and water. Then my partner prepared the vegetables while I worked on the dough.
Tutor: Did you put the bread straight into the oven?
Nora: No. We left it for thirty minutes first. After that, we baked it for twenty-five minutes.
Tutor: And the salad?
Nora: We washed the vegetables, cut them into small pieces and put them in a large bowl. We added the oil just before we served it.
Tutor: What went wrong?
Nora: We made too much salad. There were four of us, but we prepared enough for six people.
Tutor: Was the bread successful?
Nora: Yes, although the outside was a little dark. Next time, we will check it earlier. Our main problem was the quantity of salad, not the bread.


#### Reading questions and answer rationales

##### EX03-R01 · `short-answer`

Why did Dan join the class? Use up to SIX WORDS for this formative question.

**Answer:** to avoid expensive ready-made food

**Why:** The reason is in the opening sentence; this longer limit is teaching-specific, not a claimed IELTS default.

##### EX03-R02 · `ordering`

Put these actions in order: add water; wash vegetables; cook onions; heat oil.

**Answer:** wash vegetables → heat oil → cook onions → add water

**Why:** This is the stated cooking sequence.

##### EX03-R03 · `short-answer`

For how many minutes were the onions cooked before the other vegetables were added?

**Answer:** five / 5

**Why:** Twenty minutes refers to the later soup stage.

##### EX03-R04 · `truth`

Each pair chose a different recipe. TRUE, FALSE or NOT GIVEN?

**Answer:** FALSE

**Why:** Everyone received the same recipe, with a choice of one extra vegetable.

##### EX03-R05 · `short-answer`

How many portions did the recipe make?

**Answer:** four / 4

**Why:** The recipe made four portions, not two.

##### EX03-R06 · `truth`

Dan added extra salt after speaking to the teacher. TRUE, FALSE or NOT GIVEN?

**Answer:** FALSE

**Why:** He tasted again and decided not to add more.

##### EX03-R07 · `short-answer`

What was Dan doing while the soup cooked?

**Answer:** cutting bread

**Why:** The passage contrasts his action with his partner setting the table.

##### EX03-R08 · `choice`

Which best describes the class: competitive, practical, or secretive?

**Answer:** practical

**Why:** It developed usable skills and explicitly was not a competition.


#### Listening questions and answer rationales

##### EX03-A01 · `choice`

Why did Nora start with the bread: it was more expensive, it needed longer, or the vegetables were unavailable?

**Answer:** it needed longer

**Why:** Nora explicitly gives the time requirement.

##### EX03-A02 · `short-answer`

What was mixed with flour? ONE WORD.

**Answer:** water

**Why:** The first preparation step names flour and water.

##### EX03-A03 · `short-answer`

How long was the bread left before baking? Give a number in minutes.

**Answer:** 30

**Why:** This is distinct from the twenty-five-minute baking period.

##### EX03-A04 · `short-answer`

How long was the bread baked? Give a number in minutes.

**Answer:** 25

**Why:** The second duration refers to baking.

##### EX03-A05 · `choice`

When was oil added: before washing, during chopping, or just before serving?

**Answer:** just before serving

**Why:** The exact timing is stated near the end of the process.

##### EX03-A06 · `short-answer`

How many people actually ate the meal?

**Answer:** four / 4

**Why:** Six is the number for whom they accidentally prepared enough salad.

##### EX03-A07 · `choice`

What was the main problem: salad quantity, burnt bread, or missing oil?

**Answer:** salad quantity

**Why:** Nora explicitly contrasts the main problem with the bread.

##### EX03-A08 · `short-answer`

What will they do earlier next time? Use up to THREE WORDS.

**Answer:** check the bread

**Why:** The future adjustment is to check the bread earlier.


#### Speaking

Describe a meal you made or an imaginary meal. Explain the sequence and one problem. Speak for 45–70 seconds. Answer: What would you do differently next time?


#### Writing

Write 70–100 words about a cooking activity. Use past simple for the main events and one while-clause for a simultaneous action.


##### Original model — show after submission

Yesterday, my friend and I made soup. First, we washed and chopped the vegetables. We heated a little oil and cooked the onions. Then we added the other vegetables and some water. While the soup was cooking, I cut the bread and my friend set the table. We made four portions, although only two people were eating. We put the extra soup in containers. The meal tasted good, but next time we will use a smaller recipe.


#### Design and assessment note

The instructional content is a fictional cooking account, not food-safety guidance. Grammar targets are past sequence, while and clear referents. Keep short-answer rules explicit; do not mark a semantically equivalent formative answer wrong merely because it is not verbatim.


**Evidence for the operations, not certification of this pack:** I02, I03, I04, I05, I06, I07, R01, R03, R04, R06, R07. See the source ledger in README.md.

<summary>EX04: Reading food labels without overgeneralising</summary>

### EX04 — Reading food labels without overgeneralising

Original Vocora-commissioned fictional teaching material; not an IELTS test or a certified band exemplar.

Associated design lesson: **L0241**. Status: **authored reference pack, not a complete runtime lesson**.

#### Target lexicon

| Target | Role | Meaning | Original example |

|---|---|---|---|

| nutrition | uncountable noun | the process or study of obtaining and using food | The course introduces nutrition. |

| nutrient | count noun | a substance in food that the body uses | The lesson compares nutrients. |

| protein | noun | a nutrient needed for growth and repair | The label lists protein. |

| carbohydrate | noun | a nutrient category that includes sugars and starches | The table includes carbohydrate. |

| fat | noun | a nutrient found in foods such as oil and butter | The label shows the amount of fat. |

| fibre | uncountable noun | plant material in food that is not fully digested | The cereal contains fibre. |



**Word partners:** food label; portion size; rich in fibre


#### Reading stimulus

A community class asked its members to compare two imaginary breakfast cereals. The activity was designed to teach careful reading of labels, not to recommend a particular food. Each label gave the amount of several nutrients in a serving. However, the serving sizes were different: a serving of Cereal A was 40 grams, whereas a serving of Cereal B was 60 grams.

Several learners initially compared the figures directly and concluded that B contained more of every nutrient. The tutor asked them to check the serving sizes first. A fair comparison required the same quantity of each cereal. The learners therefore converted the figures to amounts per 100 grams before discussing the differences.

The class also examined the language on the front of each packet. Both products were described as natural, but the exercise provided no definition of that term. The tutor explained that the word alone did not establish which product would suit a particular person. The learners needed to identify the actual information available and separate it from an attractive description.

Finally, the groups wrote a short explanation for another learner. They were asked to say what could be concluded from the labels and what remained unknown. The labels did not describe the rest of a person's diet, their preferences or their individual needs. The class therefore avoided declaring one cereal the best choice for everyone. Its conclusion was narrower: comparisons are clearer when the quantities match and claims are supported by the information shown.


#### Listening script — audio not yet recorded

Tutor: What did your group notice about the two labels?
Maya: At first, we thought Cereal B had less sugar because its front label said light.
Tutor: Did the word light explain the sugar content?
Maya: No. We checked the numbers instead. Then we noticed that the serving sizes were different.
Owen: We nearly compared forty grams of A with sixty grams of B. We changed both to one hundred grams.
Tutor: Good. What happened to your conclusion?
Owen: It became more limited. We could compare the figures, but we could not say which cereal was best for every person.
Maya: We also wanted to compare price. A cost three pounds a packet and B cost four, but the packets were different sizes.
Tutor: How could you compare the prices more fairly?
Maya: By calculating the cost for the same weight.
Tutor: Exactly. What information was still missing?
Owen: We did not know what else a person ate. We also did not know which product they preferred.
Tutor: Then include those limits in your explanation. The aim is not to choose a universal winner; it is to make a justified comparison.


#### Reading questions and answer rationales

##### EX04-R01 · `short-answer`

What was the serving size of Cereal A? Write a number and unit.

**Answer:** 40 grams

**Why:** The first paragraph gives the two different serving sizes.

##### EX04-R02 · `short-answer`

What common quantity was used for comparison?

**Answer:** 100 grams

**Why:** The learners converted the figures to amounts per 100 grams.

##### EX04-R03 · `truth`

The exercise recommended one cereal for all consumers. TRUE, FALSE or NOT GIVEN?

**Answer:** FALSE

**Why:** The passage explicitly avoids a universal recommendation.

##### EX04-R04 · `truth`

The activity defined the word natural precisely. TRUE, FALSE or NOT GIVEN?

**Answer:** FALSE

**Why:** It says no definition was provided.

##### EX04-R05 · `truth`

Cereal A tasted sweeter than Cereal B. TRUE, FALSE or NOT GIVEN?

**Answer:** NOT GIVEN

**Why:** Taste was not reported.

##### EX04-R06 · `choice`

The main purpose of the passage is to explain cooking, label comparison, or food storage.

**Answer:** label comparison

**Why:** All paragraphs concern evaluating label information and its limits.

##### EX04-R07 · `short-answer`

In they were asked in the final paragraph, who does they refer to?

**Answer:** the groups

**Why:** The previous sentence identifies the groups writing explanations.

##### EX04-R08 · `rewrite`

Rewrite without changing scope: The labels did not tell us everything about a person's diet.

**Answer:** The labels provided incomplete information about a person's diet.

**Why:** A valid paraphrase must preserve the limitation, not claim that the labels contain no information.


#### Listening questions and answer rationales

##### EX04-A01 · `choice`

What first led Maya to a conclusion about sugar: the numbers, the word light, or the price?

**Answer:** the word light

**Why:** She initially relied on front-of-packet wording.

##### EX04-A02 · `short-answer`

What quantity did they finally use for both products?

**Answer:** 100 grams

**Why:** Owen explicitly states the corrected common quantity.

##### EX04-A03 · `truth`

The group concluded that one cereal was best for everyone. TRUE or FALSE?

**Answer:** FALSE

**Why:** Owen says they could not make that universal claim.

##### EX04-A04 · `short-answer`

What else did Maya want to compare? ONE WORD.

**Answer:** price

**Why:** She introduces a separate price comparison.

##### EX04-A05 · `short-answer`

What was the price of packet A? Give a number in pounds.

**Answer:** 3

**Why:** Four pounds is B's packet price.

##### EX04-A06 · `choice`

Why could packet prices not be compared directly: different weights, different shops, or different currencies?

**Answer:** different weights

**Why:** Maya says the packets were different sizes.

##### EX04-A07 · `short-answer`

Name ONE kind of missing personal information.

**Answer:** diet / preferences

**Why:** Owen names what else a person ate and which product they preferred.

##### EX04-A08 · `choice`

The tutor wants a universal ranking, an attractive advertisement, or a justified comparison?

**Answer:** a justified comparison

**Why:** This is the tutor's final explicit statement.


#### Speaking

Explain why two labels or prices can be difficult to compare. Give an example and identify one thing that the information does not establish. Speak for 60–90 seconds.


#### Writing

Write 100–150 words explaining the label-comparison activity. Include the initial error, the correction and one limitation. Do not give medical advice or invent nutrient figures.


##### Original model — show after submission

The class compared two cereal labels, but the serving sizes were not equal. Cereal A used a 40-gram serving and B used a 60-gram serving. Comparing the displayed figures directly could therefore be misleading. The learners converted both sets of figures to amounts per 100 grams. This gave them a common basis for comparison. They also questioned general descriptions such as natural, because the exercise did not define the term. Although the labels contained useful information, they did not describe a person's complete diet or preferences. The groups therefore explained the differences without claiming that one product was best for everyone.


#### Design and assessment note

All brands and figures are fictional. This is a language and comparison exercise, not individual nutritional guidance. Teach clause/noun distinctions and mass nouns before the output; factual health implications are deliberately not assessed.


**Evidence for the operations, not certification of this pack:** I02, I03, I04, I05, I06, I07, R01, R03, R04, R06, R07. See the source ledger in README.md.

<summary>EX05: A surplus-food collection programme</summary>

### EX05 — A surplus-food collection programme

Original Vocora-commissioned fictional teaching material; not an IELTS test or a certified band exemplar.

Associated design lesson: **L0321**. Status: **authored reference pack, not a complete runtime lesson**.

#### Target lexicon

| Target | Role | Meaning | Original example |

|---|---|---|---|

| surplus | noun/adjective | more than is currently needed | The shop donated its surplus bread. |

| shortage | count noun | a situation in which there is not enough of something | A shortage of drivers delayed collection. |

| expiry | noun | the end of a stated period of validity | The form includes an expiry date. |

| storage | uncountable noun | keeping goods until they are used | The programme needs suitable storage. |

| preservation | uncountable noun | keeping something from being lost or spoiled | The discussion concerned food preservation. |

| distribution | noun | the process of giving or delivering goods to different places | Distribution took longer than collection. |



**Word partners:** surplus food; storage conditions; reduce consumption


#### Reading stimulus

A fictional town trialled a scheme for collecting surplus food from small shops. The organisers hoped to reduce the amount discarded at closing time while supplying a community kitchen. They began with four participating shops and a volunteer collection team. Each shop recorded how much food it offered and whether a volunteer collected it.

During the first month, the organisers counted every offered item as food saved. A review showed that this overstated the result: some items were not collected, and others could not be used by the kitchen. The team changed its records to distinguish food offered, food collected and food actually used. This made the results less impressive at first glance, but more informative.

The main difficulty was timing. Shops closed at different hours, and the kitchen could not receive deliveries late at night. The organisers therefore introduced two scheduled collection windows. They also asked shops to record the types and quantities of food before a driver arrived. Volunteers reported that these changes made planning easier, although they did not remove every delay.

A second issue concerned the purpose of the scheme. Some shop owners viewed donation as a solution to excess stock. The organisers agreed that redistribution could be useful, but argued that preventing avoidable surplus should remain a separate goal. A shop that ordered more accurately might donate less while also wasting less. Donation totals alone would not reveal that improvement.

At the end of the trial, the group did not claim to have eliminated food waste. It reported the quantities at each stage and described the remaining problems. The next trial would compare stock-planning support with collection support. The organisers wanted to know not only how much food moved through the programme, but why surplus arose and which changes reduced the amount that could not be used.


#### Listening script — audio not yet recorded

Coordinator: We need to agree what our report will count as a successful result.
Volunteer: Last week, the shops offered eighty boxes. Could we say that we saved eighty boxes of food?
Coordinator: Not exactly. How many were actually collected?
Volunteer: Sixty-eight. We missed one collection because the driver was unavailable.
Kitchen manager: And we used sixty of those boxes. Eight could not be included in our planned meals.
Volunteer: Then sixty is the figure for food used, not eighty.
Coordinator: Correct. We should report all three figures, with clear labels.
Kitchen manager: We also need to discuss timing. The late collection arrives after our team has finished work.
Volunteer: Could we ask every shop to close earlier?
Coordinator: That would not be realistic. I suggest moving our second collection window to six o'clock instead of eight.
Kitchen manager: Six would work better for us, provided that the delivery arrives by half past six.
Volunteer: Some shops may still have food left after that.
Coordinator: Yes, so this will be a trial rather than a complete solution. We should record what remains uncollected.
Kitchen manager: And please do not use a lower donation total as automatic evidence that a shop is doing worse. A shop might have reduced its surplus in the first place.
Coordinator: Exactly. We need to distinguish prevention from redistribution.


#### Reading questions and answer rationales

##### EX05-R01 · `choice`

The trial aimed mainly to sell food, redistribute surplus, or replace all shops?

**Answer:** redistribute surplus

**Why:** It collected surplus for a community kitchen.

##### EX05-R02 · `truth`

Every item offered was used by the kitchen. TRUE, FALSE or NOT GIVEN?

**Answer:** FALSE

**Why:** The review identified both uncollected and unusable items.

##### EX05-R03 · `short-answer`

How many collection windows were introduced?

**Answer:** two / 2

**Why:** The timing change introduced two scheduled windows.

##### EX05-R04 · `matching`

Match the measure to its meaning: offered / collected / used.

**Answer:** offered = made available; collected = picked up; used = incorporated by the kitchen

**Why:** The paragraph separates three different stages.

##### EX05-R05 · `truth`

Lower donation totals necessarily indicate more waste. TRUE, FALSE or NOT GIVEN?

**Answer:** FALSE

**Why:** Better ordering could reduce both donations and waste.

##### EX05-R06 · `short-answer`

What two forms of support will the next trial compare?

**Answer:** stock-planning support and collection support

**Why:** The final paragraph specifies the comparison.

##### EX05-R07 · `choice`

Why were the revised results more useful: larger numbers, clearer distinctions, or no remaining problems?

**Answer:** clearer distinctions

**Why:** The records became less visually impressive but more informative.

##### EX05-R08 · `truth`

The programme was cheaper than every alternative. TRUE, FALSE or NOT GIVEN?

**Answer:** NOT GIVEN

**Why:** No comparative cost evidence is supplied.


#### Listening questions and answer rationales

##### EX05-A01 · `short-answer`

Boxes offered: write a number.

**Answer:** 80

**Why:** Eighty is the offered total.

##### EX05-A02 · `short-answer`

Boxes collected: write a number.

**Answer:** 68

**Why:** Sixty-eight were actually picked up.

##### EX05-A03 · `short-answer`

Boxes used: write a number.

**Answer:** 60

**Why:** Sixty were used; eight collected boxes were not.

##### EX05-A04 · `short-answer`

Suggested time for the second collection: write a time.

**Answer:** 6:00 / six o'clock

**Why:** Eight is the previous time, explicitly replaced by six.

##### EX05-A05 · `short-answer`

Latest suitable arrival time: write a time.

**Answer:** 6:30 / half past six

**Why:** The kitchen manager makes acceptance conditional on this arrival time.

##### EX05-A06 · `choice`

Which idea is rejected: earlier shop closing, reporting three totals, or recording leftovers?

**Answer:** earlier shop closing

**Why:** The coordinator calls that proposal unrealistic.

##### EX05-A07 · `choice`

What can a lower donation total indicate: better stock planning, necessarily more waste, or a larger driver team?

**Answer:** better stock planning

**Why:** The kitchen manager explains the possibility.

##### EX05-A08 · `short-answer`

What distinction does the coordinator emphasise at the end?

**Answer:** prevention and redistribution

**Why:** These are the two explicitly contrasted aims.


#### Speaking

Describe a local scheme that tries to solve a practical problem. Explain its goal, one difficulty and a better way to measure success. Speak for up to two minutes.


#### Writing

Write 150–200 words answering: Is collecting surplus food enough to solve food waste? Use the fictional trial as an example, distinguish prevention from redistribution and acknowledge a limitation.


##### Original model — show after submission

Collecting surplus food can be useful, but it is not a complete response to food waste. In the fictional trial, donations supplied a community kitchen. However, the amount offered by shops was not the same as the amount collected or used. A programme could therefore report impressive donation figures while leaving important problems unresolved.

Better collection schedules may improve redistribution. For example, a delivery that arrives while the kitchen team is working is more likely to be useful than a late delivery. Nevertheless, redistribution addresses surplus after it has been produced. More accurate stock planning may prevent some of that surplus from arising. A shop might consequently donate less and waste less at the same time.

The programme should therefore measure several outcomes rather than reward donation totals alone. It needs records of what was offered, collected and used, alongside information about avoidable surplus. This would not guarantee that every item could be used, but it would support a more balanced evaluation.


#### Design and assessment note

The longer text is an authored learning passage, not a calibrated IELTS Reading passage. The writing task is a bridge to Task 2, not a full official-length Task 2 task. Do not advertise 150–200 words as sufficient for the real Task 2.


**Evidence for the operations, not certification of this pack:** I02, I03, I04, I05, I06, I07, R01, R03, R04, R06, R07. See the source ledger in README.md.
